t.3.35.1: Having heard those words of the lord of the rākṣasas, the greatly wise Mārīca, skilled in speech, replied to the sovereign of the rākṣasas.
t.3.35.2: O king, men who always speak pleasing words are easy to find, but one who speaks what is unpleasant yet beneficial, and one who listens to it, are hard to find.
t.3.35.3: Surely you do not know Rāma, of great valor and exalted in virtues, equal to great Indra and Varuṇa, for you are rash and have no spies at work.
t.3.35.4: Is all well, my dear, with all the rākṣasas on earth? Surely Rāma, enraged, would not make the world empty of rākṣasas?
t.3.35.5: Has Janaka's daughter not been born to bring about the end of your life? And may not a great calamity arise with Sītā as its cause?
t.3.35.6: Having gained you as its lord, one who acts at the whim of desire and knows no restraint, will not the city of Laṅkā perish together with you and all its rākṣasas?
t.3.35.7: For a king like you, given over to desire, of wicked conduct, counselled by evil men, that foolish king destroys himself, his own people, and his kingdom.
t.3.35.8: He has not been cast off by his father, nor is he in any way one who transgresses the bounds of propriety; he is not greedy, nor of wicked conduct, nor a disgrace to the kṣatriyas.
t.3.35.9: Nor is he, who increases the joy of Kausalyā, lacking in righteousness and virtues; nor is he harsh toward living beings, but is devoted to the welfare of all.
t.3.35.10: Seeing his truthful father deceived by Kaikeyī, the righteous one said, "I will do it," and then went forth into the forest.
t.3.35.11: To fulfil the wish dear to Kaikeyī and to his father Daśaratha, he gave up the kingdom and its pleasures and entered the Daṇḍaka forest.
t.3.35.12: Rāma is not harsh, my dear, nor ignorant, nor lacking mastery over his senses. No falsehood has ever been heard of him, and you ought not to speak one.
t.3.35.13: Rāma is dharma embodied, virtuous and truly valiant; he is the king of the whole world, as Vāsava is of the gods.
t.3.35.14: How can you wish to carry off by force his Vaidehī, protected by his own splendor, as one might wish to seize the radiance of Vivasvant?
t.3.35.15: You ought not to enter the fire that is Rāma, suddenly blazing in battle, irresistible, whose flames are arrows and whose fuel is bow and sword.
t.3.35.16: Him whose bent bow is a blazing, gaping mouth and whose arrows are its flames, the unforgiving hero who bears bow and arrows and sweeps away the armies of his foes.
t.3.35.17: Abandoning your kingdom and happiness, and your own cherished life, you ought not, dear one, to assail here Rāma, who is Death itself.
t.3.35.18: Immeasurable indeed is the splendour of him whose wife is that daughter of Janaka; you are not able to carry her off in the forest, for she has the shelter of Rāma's bow.
t.3.35.19: Sītā, the slender-waisted, is his wife, dearer to him even than his life-breaths, ever devoted to him, like the flame of a blazing fire.
t.3.35.21: He, having taken counsel together with all his ministers, most devoted to dharma and headed by Vibhīṣaṇa, and having made his own resolve,
t.3.35.20: What will you gain, lord of the rākṣasas, by making this futile effort? If you are seen in battle, then that will be the end of your life; and life, happiness and kingship are all very hard to come by.
t.3.35.22: Having weighed the strength and weakness of the faults and the merits, and having truly understood your own strength and that of Rāghava, and having determined what is indeed good for you, you ought to do what is fitting.
t.3.35.23: But I think that a clash in battle with the son of the Kosala king is not fitting for you. Hear once more these excellent words, which are proper and fitting, O lord of the night-wanderers.
